title: Nutrition screening and support
blurb: Screen with 'MUST', recognise malnutrition and refeeding risk, and help people eat and drink safely.
question: Mr Dlamini, 71, is admitted with a chest infection. His BMI is 19 kg/m² and he has lost 7% of his body weight unintentionally over 4 months. He is eating well today. What is his 'MUST' score and risk category?

teach.h: Malnutrition is common and often missed
teach.body: Malnutrition is a state in which a lack of energy, protein or other nutrients causes measurable harm to body function, recovery and outcome. NICE CG32 defines a person as malnourished if their BMI is under 18.5 kg/m², they have lost more than 10% of their weight unintentionally in 3–6 months, or their BMI is under 20 with more than 5% weight loss in 3–6 months. In plain English: thin, losing weight, or not eating for days means act now.

teach.caption: BAPEN 'Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool'. High risk: refer to dietitian or nutrition support team, set goals, monitor weekly in hospital.

teach.body: BMI 19 kg/m² scores 1 (18.5–20). A 7% unplanned weight loss in 3–6 months scores 1 (5–10%). He is eating today, so the acute disease effect scores 0. Total 2: high risk. The nurse records the score, refers him to the dietitian (or follows local policy), starts a food and fluid chart, offers snacks and nourishing drinks he likes, and plans weekly rescreening while he is in hospital.

bands.label: Low: routine care; rescreen weekly in hospital
Medium: observe; record intake for 3 days
High: treat; refer to dietitian, set goals

items: Ask about preferences, culture, religion and usual eating pattern; record special diets.
Sit the person up, clean hands, dentures in and fitting, glasses on, food within reach.
Offer modified cutlery, plate guards or adapted cups for people who can chew and swallow but struggle to feed themselves (CG32).
Help those who cannot feed themselves, at their pace (a fundamental of care in the Code).
Watch for coughing, choking or a wet voice when eating: refer to a swallowing specialist (CG32 dysphagia indicators).
Record what was actually eaten, not what was served.

values: Little or none for over 10 days

values: Low K, phosphate or Mg before feeding

teach.caption: High risk: start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day and give thiamin and vitamin B before and during the first 10 days. Eaten little for over 5 days (not high risk): start at no more than 50% of requirements for the first 2 days.

teach.h: Supplements are part of a plan
teach.body: Oral nutritional supplements help people who can swallow safely and are malnourished or at risk, but only if they are taken. If bottles are left unopened, find out why (taste, timing, fullness, nausea) and review the plan with the dietitian rather than just recording 'declined'. Supplements are not a substitute for help at mealtimes, and NICE CG179 does not recommend them specifically to prevent pressure ulcers if intake is already adequate.

teach.text: A normal-looking or even overweight person can still be malnourished: 'MUST' scores weight loss and the effect of acute illness, not just BMI. And a starving person is at risk from feeding too fast: check refeeding risk before nutrition support starts.

items: Screen inpatients on admission and weekly (CG32), using 'MUST'.
'MUST': BMI score + weight loss score + acute disease effect; 0 low, 1 medium, 2 or more high.
Malnourished: BMI under 18.5; over 10% loss in 3–6 months; or BMI under 20 with over 5% loss.
Refeeding high risk: start at most 10 kcal/kg/day with thiamin; little intake for 5 days: no more than 50% for 2 days.
Help people eat: positioning, aids, assistance, record intake, refer if swallowing problems.

summary: You can now calculate a 'MUST' score and act on its risk category, apply NICE CG32 criteria for malnutrition and refeeding risk, and give practical help with eating and drinking, including recognising when to refer a swallowing problem.

A.q: Mrs Webb, 78, is admitted to a medical ward with a chest infection. Under NICE CG32, when should she be screened for malnutrition while an inpatient?
options: On admission, then weekly
Within 72 hours, then monthly
When she starts losing weight
On admission and at discharge
A.why: NICE CG32: all hospital inpatients should be screened on admission and weekly thereafter.

whyNot.1: 72 hours and monthly do not match CG32's admission and weekly schedule.
whyNot.2: Waiting for weight loss misses those already at risk.
whyNot.3: Screening at discharge alone misses deterioration during the stay.

A.q: Which finding meets the NICE CG32 definition of malnourished?
options: BMI of 19 kg/m² with stable weight
Weight loss of 4% over the last 6 months
BMI under 18.5 kg/m²
Eating half of meals for the past 3 days
A.why: CG32 rec 1.3.1: BMI under 18.5 kg/m² defines malnutrition (as do over 10% loss in 3–6 months, or BMI under 20 with over 5% loss).

whyNot.0: BMI 19 with stable weight does not meet the definition.
whyNot.1: 4% is below both CG32 weight-loss thresholds.
whyNot.3: Three days of reduced intake does not meet the 5-day at-risk threshold.

A.q: Mr Evans, 80, has Parkinson's disease. His tremor makes it hard to get food to his mouth and he is eating less than half his meals. Which intervention should come first?
options: Prescribe oral supplements three times daily
Provide adapted cutlery and help at meals
Ask his family to bring in his favourite foods
Refer him for a nasogastric feeding tube
A.why: CG32: offer appropriate support, such as modified eating aids, for people who can chew and swallow but cannot feed themselves easily. This tackles the cause.

whyNot.0: Supplements may help later, but the barrier is getting food to his mouth.
whyNot.2: Favourite foods help appetite but do not solve the feeding difficulty.
whyNot.3: Tube feeding is not indicated when he can swallow and could eat with help.

B.q: Mr Dlamini, 71, has a BMI of 19 kg/m² and an unplanned 7% weight loss over 4 months. He is eating normally today. What is his 'MUST' score?
options: 1, medium risk
3, high risk
0, low risk
2, high risk
B.why: BMI 18.5–20 scores 1; 5–10% weight loss scores 1; no acute disease effect scores 0. Total 2 = high risk (BAPEN 'MUST').

whyNot.0: This counts only one of the two scoring factors.
whyNot.1: The acute disease effect does not apply because he is eating.
whyNot.2: Both BMI and weight loss score points.

B.q: Ms Lyon, 45, has a history of alcohol misuse, a BMI of 17.5 kg/m² and has eaten almost nothing for 7 days. Nutrition support is planned. What does NICE CG32 recommend?
options: Start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day with thiamin
Start at full requirements to correct the deficit fast
Start at no more than 50% of requirements for 2 days
Delay feeding until her electrolytes are fully normal
B.why: Two high-risk criteria (BMI under 18.5, little intake over 5 days, alcohol misuse: three here) make her high refeeding risk: start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day and give thiamin and vitamin B (CG32).

whyNot.1: Full feeding in a high-risk person risks refeeding syndrome.
whyNot.2: 50% for 2 days applies to people who have eaten little for 5 days without high-risk criteria.
whyNot.3: CG32 corrects electrolytes alongside cautious feeding rather than delaying it.

B.q: Mrs Rao, 74, has oral supplements prescribed twice daily. On the ward round the nurse sees the bottles left unopened on her table each day. What is most appropriate?
options: Record them as declined and continue to offer them
Explore why and review the plan with the dietitian
Ask the doctor to prescribe a nasogastric tube feed instead
Increase the supplements to three times a day
B.why: Supplements only help if taken. Explore barriers (taste, timing, fullness, nausea) and review the plan with the dietitian and with her.

whyNot.0: Recording refusal without exploring the reason leaves the problem unsolved.
whyNot.2: A tube is a big step when the cause of refusal is unknown.
whyNot.3: More of an untaken supplement achieves nothing.

C.q: Mr Hayes, 66, is drowsy after surgery and has had no food for 6 days. His BMI is 23 kg/m² and he has no other refeeding risk factors. Nutrition support is planned. What does NICE CG32 recommend for the first 2 days?
options: Full estimated requirements from the start
A maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day with thiamin
No more than 50% of estimated requirements
Oral fluids until he is fully awake
C.why: CG32: people who have eaten little or nothing for more than 5 days should have nutrition support at no more than 50% of requirements for the first 2 days.

whyNot.0: Starting at full requirements after 6 days without food risks refeeding problems.
whyNot.1: 10 kcal/kg/day is for high refeeding risk, which he does not meet.
whyNot.3: He is drowsy, so oral fluids may be unsafe, and this delays nutrition support.

C.q: Mrs Kemp, 82, eats well but coughs and her voice sounds wet after each drink. Her BMI is 22 kg/m². What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give thickened drinks routinely to everyone at risk
Refer her to a swallowing specialist for assessment
Start oral supplements to keep her intake up
Encourage her to drink faster to finish quickly
C.why: Coughing or a wet voice with drinking are dysphagia indicators; CG32 asks for referral to a professional skilled in swallowing assessment.

whyNot.0: Thickening should follow individual assessment, not be applied routinely.
whyNot.2: Supplements do not address an unsafe swallow.

C.q: Mr Okoro, 58, is acutely unwell in critical care and is not expected to eat for more than 5 days. His BMI is 24 kg/m² and his weight is stable. What is his 'MUST' score?
options: 0, low risk
2, high risk
1, medium risk
4, high risk
C.why: BMI over 20 scores 0, no weight loss scores 0, but the acute disease effect (acutely ill with no intake likely for more than 5 days) adds 2. Total 2 = high risk.

whyNot.0: This misses the acute disease effect.
whyNot.2: The acute disease effect scores 2, not 1.
whyNot.3: Only the acute disease effect scores here.

reteach.title: Three questions in 'MUST'
reteach.question: If you had no chart in front of you, what three questions would tell you whether someone is at nutritional risk?

blocks.body: Is the person thin now (BMI)? Have they been losing weight without trying (weight loss over 3–6 months)? Are they so unwell that they have eaten or will eat nothing for more than 5 days (acute disease effect)? 'MUST' turns those three questions into points; any two points means high risk and action.

blocks.text: The acute disease effect scores 2 or nothing; there is no 1. A score of 2 from that alone already means high risk.

explain.body: CG32: inpatients on admission and weekly; outpatients at first appointment; care homes on admission and with concern; GP at registration and with concern. Use a validated tool such as 'MUST'.

test.q: When should a care home resident be screened for malnutrition under NICE CG32?
options: Monthly, whatever their condition
Every 6 months as a routine check
When a GP requests a screen
On admission and with any concern
test.why: CG32: care home residents are screened on admission and when there is clinical concern.

whyNot.0: Monthly rescreening is a 'MUST' follow-up interval for some risk levels, not the CG32 trigger.
whyNot.2: Screening is a nursing responsibility, not dependent on a GP request.

explain.body: BMI over 20 = 0, 18.5–20 = 1, under 18.5 = 2. Weight loss under 5% = 0, 5–10% = 1, over 10% = 2. Acute disease effect = 2. Total 0 low, 1 medium, 2 or more high.

test.q: A BMI of 17.8 kg/m² scores how many points in step 1 of 'MUST'?

whyNot.3: The highest BMI score in 'MUST' is 2.

explain.body: High risk with one of: BMI under 16, loss over 15%, little intake over 10 days, low K/phosphate/Mg; or two of: BMI under 18.5, loss over 10%, little intake over 5 days, alcohol misuse or drugs like insulin or diuretics. Start at most 10 kcal/kg/day with thiamin.

test.q: Which single finding alone places a person at high refeeding risk under CG32?
options: BMI of 17 kg/m²
Little intake for 6 days
BMI under 16 kg/m²
Weight loss of 12%
test.why: A BMI under 16 kg/m² is one of the single criteria for high refeeding risk.

whyNot.0: BMI under 18.5 counts only with a second criterion.
whyNot.1: Over 5 days counts only with a second criterion; alone it needs over 10 days.
whyNot.3: Over 10% counts only with a second criterion; alone it needs over 15%.

explain.body: Position upright, dentures and glasses in, food within reach, adapted aids if needed, help for those who cannot feed themselves. Record what is eaten. Coughing, choking or a wet voice when eating or drinking means refer for swallowing assessment.

test.q: Which sign during a meal suggests a swallowing problem needing referral?
options: Choosing to eat in the day room
Leaving vegetables uneaten
Asking for the salt and pepper
Coughing after each mouthful
test.why: Coughing or choking during or after swallowing is a CG32 indicator of dysphagia that needs specialist referral.

whyNot.0: Where someone prefers to eat is a personal choice, not an indicator of dysphagia.
whyNot.1: Food preference does not suggest a swallowing problem.
whyNot.2: Wanting seasoning reflects taste, not difficulty swallowing.
